analysis.one_liner: Blocks companies from using or selling people's health and location data without consent.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Klobuchar with 2 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop commercial companies from collecting, keeping, or sharing personal health data unless the person gave express written consent or the data was strictly needed to provide the requested service. It would ban using health data for advertising and ban data brokers from selling location data — including data from fitness trackers, web browsing, and visits near medical centers. People would get the right to see and delete their data, and the Federal Trade Commission and private lawsuits would enforce the rules. Companies whose violations broke the law could face fines up to 15% of their parent company's annual revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose phone, apps, fitness tracker, or browsing history can reveal health information — for example, searches for mental health care, pregnancy, or addiction treatment. The bill would give them consent rights, access and deletion rights, and a way to sue violators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People using health apps and wearables

how_it_helps.text: Companies could not collect, retain, use, or disclose personal health data except with a person's express written consent or as strictly necessary to provide the requested product or service.
The bill bans using health data — from any source, including wearables and web browsing — for commercial advertising.
Data brokers could not sell location data, and no one could sell location data to a data broker, closing a market that lets companies buy people's movements near clinics and places of worship.

Individuals would gain enforceable rights to access and delete their health and location data within 15 days, at no charge, and violations would count as concrete injury allowing private lawsuits with damages of $100 to $1,000 per violation per day.
Pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers would be unenforceable for claims under the bill, so people could band together in court.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, digital advertising companies, and app and wearable makers that monetize health and location data would lose a revenue stream and face FTC enforcement, lawsuits, and penalties up to 15% of their parent company's prior-year revenue.

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts HIPAA-covered health providers, insurance plans, and their business associates, so much health data held by doctors and insurers stays under older, narrower rules rather than gaining the bill's consent and deletion rights.

The definition of health data includes information inferred or extrapolated from non-health data, so ordinary browsing and app activity could fall under strict new rules, and honest supporters would acknowledge the compliance burden this creates for startups and smaller app makers.
The private right of action with per-day damages and a 6-year statute of limitations could generate substantial litigation, a cost an honest supporter would weigh against the privacy benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections are strong and directly aimed at a real harm — companies selling or targeting ads with data that reveals health conditions and movements. The main gaps are that HIPAA-covered providers and insurers are exempt, leaving a large slice of health data under older rules, and the broad definitions plus potent private lawsuits would impose real compliance and litigation costs on companies of all sizes. On balance the consumer protections outweigh those costs, but the design is not airtight.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the UPHOLD Privacy Act on March 2, 2023, joined by Sens. Warren and Hirono.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
The bill received no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and advertising-driven tech companies kept their ability to buy, sell, and target people's health and location data, and consumers gained no new federal protections in this area.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restrict commercial use of health data and the sale of location data by brokers.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing or a committee vote.

sides.party_line_note: The only supporters on record were three Senate Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican- and Democrat-led committee process never moved the bill, so it ended without any recorded votes.

industries.note: The bill outlaws their core business of selling location data, including data from fitness trackers and browsing history, and threatens penalties up to 15% of a violator's parent-company revenue. Brokers profit by trading Americans' movements, which the bill would shut down.
The bill bans using health data for commercial advertising, cutting off targeted health-related ad revenue. Their gain comes at the expense of people whose sensitive data fuels the targeting.

They could keep using health data strictly to provide requested services but would face consent requirements, privacy-policy and access/deletion duties, and litigation exposure. Consumers would gain rights over the same data these companies hold.

The bill exempts entities covered by HIPAA and their business associates, leaving them under existing rules rather than the bill's stricter consent regime. Their established role as holders of health data stays in place.
